result.summary: Ovid's argument recounts how Juno had Ilithyia obstruct Alcmena's labour until her maid Galanthis tricked the goddess and was turned into a weasel. Alcmena then tells the story to Iole, who is about to give birth to Hyllus's child.

scenes.title: Argument: Galanthis becomes a weasel
scenes.summary: The prefatory argument summarises Juno's spite, Lucina's delaying spell, Galanthis's trick and her transformation.
scenes.stakes: Alcmena's life and the birth of Hercules are at risk from Juno's revenge.

scenes.title: Alcmena confides in Iole
scenes.summary: Eurystheus still hates Hercules. The aged Alcmena finds comfort in Iole, wife of Hyllus, and begins her tale with a blessing for Iole's coming labour.
scenes.stakes: Alcmena faces the anxiety and loneliness of old age.

scenes.title: Alcmena's agonising labour
scenes.summary: Alcmena recalls seven days of torment as Lucina, corrupted by Juno, sat on the altar with crossed knees and fingers and muttered charms.
scenes.stakes: Alcmena's life, in agony from the delayed birth, is threatened by Juno's vengeance.

scenes.title: Galanthis tricks the goddess
scenes.summary: Galanthis falsely announces the birth. Lucina leaps up, breaking the spell, and Hercules is born. The goddess punishes Galanthis by turning her into a weasel.
scenes.stakes: Galanthis risks the wrath of a goddess for her mistress.

alias_notes.explanation: Lucina is the Roman name of the birth goddess; Ilithyia is the Greek form.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains the weasel's supposed mouth-birth as punishment for Galanthis's lying mouth.

analysis.text: The tale shows divine jealousy and a clever mortal's trick, ending in a punitive transformation typical of the Metamorphoses.
Ovid draws on an ancient belief that weasels bore their young through the mouth, offering a mythic explanation for it.

fun_facts.text: The crossed legs and clasped fingers of Lucina reflect the ancient belief that knots and crossed limbs could bind or delay birth.

language_notes.text: Ilithyïa is the Greek goddess of childbirth, identified with the Roman Lucina; the text uses both names for the same goddess.
This line links to Hercules' labours: Atlas had felt the weight of Hercules when the hero briefly held up the heavens. The footnote [29] marks an editor's note.
Awkward syntax: Alcmena 'has Iole' as someone to whom she can confide her complaints, achievements and misfortunes.
The 'tenth sign' refers to the tenth month; the 'luminary' is the sun. The sense is that she was in her tenth month of pregnancy, and the child was unusually heavy.
The Nixi were minor birth deities who aided women in labour, invoked together with Lucina.
Crossed knees and interlaced fingers were folk-magic gestures believed to block or delay birth.
Cadmeian means Theban, from Cadmus, the legendary founder of Thebes, where Alcmena lived.
Ancient belief held that weasels gave birth through the mouth, so Galanthis's punishment mirrors her lying mouth.

context_notes.text: Eurystheus was the king who imposed the twelve labours on Hercules, and he hated him as Juno's favourite agent.
Hyllus was the son of Hercules and Deianira; Iole was a princess Hercules had captured and then gave to Hyllus.
Juno hated Alcmena because Jupiter had fathered Hercules by her, and so she turned the birth goddess against her.

literary_notes.text: The cold shudder shows that remembered pain still grips the old woman, bringing the past into the present.
Words that would move hard stones exaggerate the pathos of Alcmena's laments.
Galanthis laughs at her trick, but the goddess seizes her mid-laugh, so her triumph turns at once into punishment.
The lying mouth that brought a false birth is punished by a transformation in which the mouth is linked to birth.
